title: Two more Chicago immigration judges fired as court becomes epicenter of removal orders
description:
It didn’t take Eva Saltzman very long to pack up a decade’s worth of material from her tenure as an immigration judge.
She is one of two judges fired Thursday from Chicago’s Immigration Court, which has seen seismic changes since President Donald Trump returned to office.
Saltzman’s time with the court coincided with explosive growth in the country’s national immigration caseload.
That was true of Judges Crites and Saltzman as well, but the Tribune analysis found that they still lagged their peers’ prolific pace of removal orders.
Judge Saltzman issued the fewest removal orders in the group, just 33 in an immigration courthouse where judges typically issued hundreds that month and where one judge issued more than 900.
text:
It didn’t take Eva Saltzman very long to pack up a decade’s worth of material from her tenure as an immigration judge.

Less than 24 hours after she received an emailed termination notice in the middle of a hearing, Saltzman stood with a carful of office supplies, art and certificates, trying to think through the fact that her time on the bench had come to an end.

She is one of two judges fired Thursday from Chicago’s Immigration Court, which has seen seismic changes since President Donald Trump returned to office. The local court has recently become the national leader in deportation orders.

Saltzman had been with the court since 2016; one of the items she brought home Friday was the framed certification bearing then-Attorney General Loretta Lynch’s signature. The second judge fired Thursday, Elizabeth Crites, had been there since 2021.

According to the National Association of Immigration Judges, another judge was fired in June, continuing a wave of firings, resignations and buyouts from the Chicago bench as Trump, who has direct oversight of the country’s immigration courts, seeks to reshape them in the image of his hard-line agenda.

Advocates, attorneys and ex-judges all say the changing lineup on the immigration bench, combined with changes to many of the basic elements that define the life of an immigration case, have all helped transform Chicago’s court into the national epicenter of removal orders: from issuing 35 a day on average during President Joe Biden’s final year in office to more than 125 a day this year.

Jeremiah Johnson, the executive vice president of the National Association of Immigration Judges and himself a recently terminated judge, referred to the exodus as a “purge” and added in a message to the Tribune that the firing of “experienced immigration judges without cause is another example of the attack on the independence of our immigration courts.”

A representative with the Executive Office for Immigration Review, which runs the country’s immigration courts as part of the U.S. Department of Justice, said the office didn’t comment on personnel matters.

Crites, reached by phone, confirmed she’d been fired but made no other comment.

Saltzman, for her part, said she had been stunned by the firing, but not necessarily surprised.

“I’ve served as an immigration judge for the last decade, and, under this administration, I continued to do my job the way I’ve always done it, giving careful consideration to each case and applying the law to each case,” she said. “And I’ve long anticipated that under this administration, performing my duties in this way may result in my termination.”

That said, she continued, there had been no immediate warning signs that she was about to be terminated.

On Friday morning, outside the Loop high-rise that’s home to most of Chicago’s immigration proceedings, Saltzman thought about what the rest of the day might look like. She’d have dinner with one of her daughters and some friends, she said. There would be more time to train for an open-water sprint triathlon, the first she’s attempted.

Saltzman’s time with the court coincided with explosive growth in the country’s national immigration caseload. But over the last few months, the court in some ways became busier still as Trump administration officials pushed to cut down a case backlog still topping 3 million, per the immigration data clearinghouse TRAC.

The Tribune reported earlier this month how Chicago’s immigration court had become the national epicenter of removal orders across the country, using Department of Justice data — obtained and refined by the research group Deportation Data Project — to find that even Biden-era judges saw notable swings toward issuing higher rates of removal orders once Trump took office.

That was true of Judges Crites and Saltzman as well, but the Tribune analysis found that they still lagged their peers’ prolific pace of removal orders.

When looking at all judges who concluded at least 50 cases that month — and excluding cases that ended with the immigrant voluntarily deciding to leave — the analysis found these two judges had the two lowest percentages of cases concluding in the issuance of removal orders. Crites handled the court’s juvenile cases, while Saltzman was one of two judges hearing cases from the detained docket, for people who are fighting their cases while in Department of Homeland Security custody.

For Judge Crites, the analysis found that she concluded roughly a fifth of her more than 500 June cases by dismissing, terminating or otherwise closing them without issuing a removal order — the kind of nuanced ending that can frustrate those pushing for mass deportation.

Judge Saltzman issued the fewest removal orders in the group, just 33 in an immigration courthouse where judges typically issued hundreds that month and where one judge issued more than 900. Saltzman said Thursday these findings weren’t surprising to her at all, given the caseload she worked with.

Immigrants who choose to fight to stay in the U.S. from detention tend to do so because their cases stand a good chance of getting a favorable outcome, she said: “The relief applications that I am considering are self-selected in a way that makes them more likely to be cases that should be granted.”

The other consequence of Saltzman’s hearing the detained docket was that her caseload drew a substantial amount of media attention, most recently in the case of Reuben Torres Maldonado. Torres Maldonado’s 16-year-old daughter, Ofelia Torres, was in the throes of treatment for Stage 4 cancer when federal agents arrested him at the height of Operation Midway Blitz. Ofelia Torres died in February.

Saltzman, as she made the decision to release him on bond Oct. 30, noted he is an unlikely flight risk and has a case to potentially remain in the United States.

“I wish you much luck in the future and I wish your daughter a full recovery,” she said.

While her docket tended to attract higher-profile cases like that of the Torres family, Saltzman said she’d “never made a decision with any particular agenda or end goal in mind.”

Chicago Tribune’s Joe Mahr contributed.

text:
HARLINGEN, Texas (AP) — The Trump administration is packing immigration courtrooms and giving less lead-time on hearings in an effort to clear a decades-long backlog. The result is a historic rise in the number of people missing court dates and being immediately ordered deported as the system struggles to keep up, new data shows.

Dozens and often hundreds of immigrants’ cases a day are being assigned to individual judges in courthouses across the country, in what are known as “mega” master hearings, which have seen a significant increase this year. More than 1,300 such hearings were held in June alone, a nearly threefold jump from the previous June, according to data analyzed by Mobile Pathways, a nonprofit that tracks immigration court data to help immigrants, their lawyers and other organizations.

At the same time, the data shows, courts have severely cut the length of time many people are getting to prepare for complex immigration proceedings, from about six months to often just a little more than a month.

They’re subsequently missing hearings, receiving deportation orders and being told they’ve abandoned any asylum claims at unprecedented rates.

“The combination of collapsed lead times and packed hearing blocks is a schedule designed for people not to have their case heard,” said Bartlomiej Skorupa, chief operating officer of Mobile Pathways. “The data shows valid claims are closed before being adjudicated.”

Those who favor stricter immigration laws see the swift hearings as a course-correction for a longstanding problem.

“There’s no credibility in the system that never reaches an end,” Andrew Arthur, a fellow at the conservative Center for Immigration Studies, said.

Still, he worries that these rapid-fire hearings could affect judges’ performance.

“You don’t want to put so many cases on that the judges get burned out or that there’s a danger of denying due process to anybody,” Arthur said.

The Justice Department office that handles immigration courts said in a statement that judges were adjusting their schedules to resolve cases more quickly, while making sure all cases get handled fairly and lawfully. It said court delays harm immigrants who have valid claims, and that the public interest is served when the government deports people without legal grounds to stay.

Immigration courts are overwhelmed

Attending immigration court in Harlingen, Texas, on days where there are mega master hearings can mean waiting outside in the hot, crowded entrance for over an hour until the lobby can accommodate the next wave of people. Adults with cases often are accompanied by relatives and attorneys, and detained children are brought in with shelter case managers and legal advocates.

The courts call it a “mega” day when a judge has more than 50 cases scheduled. Although the practice is not new, it became much more frequent starting in mid-May.

On a recent day, about 90 cases were scheduled with Immigration Judge Delia Gonzalez. More than 20 people did not show up, but even so she ran out of time to hear each case and rescheduled a handful of people who had waited more than eight hours.

“There’s a real limit to how many cases a judge can hear with any care in one morning,” said former immigration judge Elizabeth Young. “When you cram that many hearings into a single docket, you’re working through a list, not holding court.”

Some immigrants requested more time before their next hearings, presenting evidence of having been defrauded by unscrupulous attorneys profiled in local news reports. Others without any attorney asked for more time to figure out the proper evidence filing procedures.

A Colombian man who submitted more than 1,500 pages as evidence in his asylum claim said he still wanted to obtain more documentation from members of the military, businesses and politicians back home.

Gonzalez declined the requests. Most cases lasted less than five minutes.

There is no leeway for no-shows

That same day in West Valley City, Utah, Immigration Judge Brock Taylor was assigned 159 cases. By noon, Taylor recited a dozen names of people from Mexico, Colombia, Peru and Venezuela who failed to show up. Without elaborating, he said each was properly notified of their hearing date and failed to appear. He ordered them removed from the United States and they would have no right to appeal.

In Chicago, attorney Peter Meinecke, a lawyer for the Resurrection Project, which runs a legal clinic for immigrants, said one of his clients was issued a removal order when he couldn’t attend a mega master hearing across the country in Seattle after a vehicle accident fractured both of his legs and confined him to a wheelchair.

At the start of the second Trump administration in January 2025, about 20% of people missed scheduled immigration court hearings nationwide, according to Mobile Pathways. As hearing notice times shrunk, that no-show rate doubled to 40% by this June, the organization said. A nonprofit group that tracks and analyzes immigration court data and gives that information to immigrants and other organizations.

Deportation orders have risen alongside the no-show rates. Almost 33,000 deportation orders were issued in January 2025. This June, there were about 79,000, according to Mobile Pathways’ data. And once a deportation order is issued, an immigrant’s asylum claim is almost always considered “abandoned.”

The national rate of cases considered abandoned is now nearly five times the historical average dating back to 2009; in New York and Chicago specifically, it’s roughly six times higher, according to Mobile Pathways.

“That’s a recipe for disaster, because more people are going to be ordered removed in absentia who truly have a valid case,” said Katie Fleming, a director at Acacia Center for Justice, a network of legal service providers.

Some people have even been issued deportation orders while they were inside the building that houses the Chicago immigration court, but confused about where to go and how to get help, according to Alex McGriff, an attorney for the National Immigrant Justice Center, which runs a legal help desk there.

“The court ordered them removed despite the fact that they were not absent,” McGriff said.

The backlog is shrinking, but caseloads are not

Advocates for stricter immigration policies call the strategy a time-saver.

“It really is economizing the judge’s time,” said Arthur, the Center for Immigration Studies fellow. “It is increasing the number of final orders that are going out, so that’s decreasing the backlog entirely.”

The backlog, which grew significantly under the Biden administration, has decreased for the first time in at least 10 years. The number of pending cases with the Executive Office of Immigration Review, which oversees immigration courts, decreased from 3.7 to 3.5 million in fiscal year 2025 and continued to drop this year.

“It can be a tough job when you’re doing it at scale,” Arthur said.

Attorneys representing immigrants have similar challenges keeping up as their own caseloads intensify.

Jaime Diez, a veteran immigration attorney based in Brownsville, Texas, recently had almost 20 cases called in one day, nearly 10 times his previously normal pace.

“Due process is being thrown out of the window,” Diez said standing outside the courtroom with a six-inch thick file for one client. “It’s very worrisome, I don’t know how long it’s going to last.”

text:
Federal judges called on the Department of Homeland Security’s top lawyer to remove social media posts naming judges who’ve ruled against the administration as the “worst of the worst.”

“I just ask our political leaders to tone it down,” Judge Esther Salas of the New Jersey federal trial court said Friday during a virtual briefing. “Criticize us on the merits, appeal us, but stop villainizing and demonizing my colleagues please.”

Salas, whose son was killed six years ago at home by a disgruntled attorney posing as a delivery man, was referencing recent posts on the social media platform X by DHS General Counsel James Percival.

Percival posted a series on July 23 titled the “Worst of the Worst, District Judge Edition,” modeled after DHS’ series highlighting the “worst of the worst” immigrants deported. The series named four federal trial judges who’ve ruled against the administration in some way over an immigration issue.

Percival, a former aide to Sen. Ashley Moody (R-Fla.) when she served as Florida attorney general, has since doubled down on the posts. He said in a video posted by DHS’ official X account on Thursday that judges are “engaging in naked politics” and “shrouding it in the thin veneer of legalese.”

“If we respond to that by saying, ‘oh wow that’s interesting, let’s analyze their legal position,’ we are legitimizing something that is not legitimate,” Percival said in the video. A DHS spokesperson also defended the posts, saying in a statement at the time that they are “accurately describing a judge’s rulings” and that “facts aren’t attacks.”

Judge Beth Bloom of the US District Court for the Southern District of Florida, who also spoke during the virtual event, said Percival’s “worst of the worst” posts are an “intimidation tactic” and should be removed. She compared the series to a “Wanted” sign featuring federal judges that was previously displayed outside a Republican lawmaker’s Capitol Hill office.

“This is not healthy criticism,” Bloom said. “These are unjustified attacks that are designed for one purpose and one purpose only, and that is to bring others to do harm. To de-legitimize not only the entire justice system but the judges who work hard every day.”

The Friday event was co-hosted by Legal AF, part of the MeidasTouch Network, and by Speak Up for Justice, a nonpartisan organization that advocates for judicial independence.

It comes amid escalating tension between the judiciary and the executive branch, as top Trump administration officials have decried court rulings that thwart President Donald Trump’s agenda.

Trump recently called the Supreme Court justices who ruled against his signature tariffs “fools” and “lapdogs,” and House Republicans have also filed impeachment resolutions against judges for ruling against the administration.

Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche also described a “war” against the federal judiciary during a conference last year, though he later claimed that his remarks “were not directed at judges.”

The American Bar Association issued a July 28 statement that condemned “personal attacks on judges by government officials.”

“Recent social media posts by an administration official criticizing judges by name are part of the growing pattern of threats, intimidation and personal attacks directed at our judiciary,” the statement said, without naming Percival or any other official.

Judges, who are permitted to speak about the independence of the judiciary under ethics rules, have increasingly pushed back against heated rhetoric. Justice Elena Kagan, testifying before congressional spending panels this month, said heated rhetoric toward judges and justices is “dangerous” to their security.

That is the reality lawmakers began to confront on July 1, when the Assembly Privacy and Consumer Protection Committee unanimously advanced SB 690 with amendments.

text:
Capitol Weekly welcomes Opinions on California public policy or politics. Please read our guidelines for opinion pieces before submitting an Op-Ed. Submissions that do not adhere to our guidelines will not be considered for publication.

OPINION — As an attorney who has spent many years litigating privacy rights, I take seriously any claim that legislation could make vulnerable families less safe.

That is why I am disappointed to see opponents of SB 690 invoke immigrant communities to defend an abusive lawsuit industry.

The facts simply do not support the argument. Of more than 4,000 California Invasion of Privacy Act (CIPA) lawsuits filed in recent years, not a single case alleges immigration-related harm, or that an immigrant was harmed, defrauded or subjected to immigration enforcement because of technology on a website.

The recent wave of CIPA litigation is not about immigration. It is not about protecting vulnerable families from bad actors — in fact, it’s quite the opposite. These lawsuits overwhelmingly target the most vulnerable entities among us: food banks, health clinics and other small businesses, nonprofits and public agencies using ordinary website technologies providing critical help, such as analytics tools, appointment scheduling software, chat features, payment processors, and other services that millions of startups, small businesses, and Californians trying to make their entrepreneurial dreams come true rely on every day.

The lawsuits even target website use of ADA accessibility tools, which are necessary for compliance, as well as cybersecurity and identity verification tools, which are necessary to prevent fraud and cyber-attacks.

Community clinics, legal aid organizations, immigrant-serving nonprofits, ethnic media outlets and advocacy organizations use these tools every day to translate information, schedule appointments, process donations, answer questions, and connect people with critical services.

In today’s legal environment, they face the very same litigation risk as the thousands of businesses, nonprofits, healthcare providers, educational institutions, and public agencies that have already been sued.

Ironically, many of the organizations opposing SB 690 have websites that rely on the very same technologies plaintiffs’ lawyers routinely characterize as illegal “wiretapping.” The opposition doesn’t even know what they’re opposing because their websites use third-party cookies and pixels without any opt-in consent.

That is the reality lawmakers began to confront on July 1, when the Assembly Privacy and Consumer Protection Committee unanimously advanced SB 690 with amendments.

The committee’s action represented an important acknowledgment that California’s 1967 wiretapping law, written decades before the internet existed, is being stretched far beyond its original purpose and used to target routine technologies that organizations rely on every day.

But there is still more work to do.

While the committee’s amendments addressed one avenue for abusive litigation, they left untouched another section in CIPA that continues to generate many of these lawsuits. As long as that loophole remains, thousands of California organizations, including small businesses, nonprofits, schools, healthcare providers, and local governments, will continue to face costly litigation over ordinary website functions.

The real winners under the current system are not immigrant families. They are a small group of plaintiffs’ lawyers who have built a lucrative business model around threatening organizations with expensive litigation.

When a neighborhood health clinic, a local legal aid organization, a family-owned restaurant, an ethnic newspaper, or a small nonprofit receives one of these demand letters, they often discover it is less expensive to settle than spend years defending themselves in court even when they have done nothing wrong.

Opponents of SB 690 have attempted to recast this debate as one about immigration, suggesting the bill would somehow expose vulnerable communities or weaken protections for sensitive personal information. That is simply not what the legislation does and that is not what we want it to do.

This bill has already seen tremendous support from immigrant-backed organizations, such as the Bay Area Hispano Institute for Advancement, California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, Hispanic Chambers of Commerce San Francisco, Latin American and Caribbean Business Chamber, Latino Restaurants Association, Latino Times newspaper, LULAC California, Solano Hispanic Chamber of Commerce and United Latinos Action.

California already has the strongest consumer privacy protections in the nation, including the California Consumer Privacy Act. SB 690 does not weaken those protections or affect immigration status.

In fact, SB 690 expressly preserves protections for sensitive immigration and medical information while ensuring that CIPA is not stretched beyond its original purpose to target ordinary website technologies.

California can protect individual privacy and protect small businesses, nonprofits, and community organizations at the same time.

The Assembly took an important first step on July 1. Now lawmakers should finish the job by closing the remaining loophole that continues to fuel abusive litigation.

Immigrant communities deserve real protections, not to be used to preserve a broken legal system.

Usama Kahf is a partner at Fisher Phillips specializing in privacy and data security.

text:
Background

ICE and TSA have expanded a data-sharing arrangement that previously focused on travelers with final orders of removal. The arrangement now extends to travelers whose authorized period of stay, as reflected on their Form I-94 Arrival/Departure Record, has expired. Notably, this includes individuals who have timely filed applications with USCIS, such as requests to extend or change nonimmigrant status, Form I-485 Adjustment of Status (“green card”) applications, or applications for asylum or other humanitarian protections, as well as individuals who hold valid employment authorization. Enforcement actions have been documented at numerous airports in recent weeks.

Historically, individuals with timely filed pending applications were not subject to enforcement action and were generally permitted to travel domestically without the risk of detention at airports absent aggravating factors such as criminal history or a prior removal order. The expansion of enforcement activity indicates that these individuals are now considered a higher priority for immigration enforcement.

How Airport Encounters Unfold

Encounters typically begin when plainclothes ICE agents approach an individual at a check-in counter, departure gate, or jet bridge. The agent already has the individual’s name, date of birth, and flight information from airline reservation data before the interaction begins. Affected individuals have reported being pulled aside in front of other passengers, separated from traveling companions (including minor children and spouses), and questioned about their immigration history. In some documented cases, individuals who presented valid Employment Authorization Documents (EADs), advance parole, and USCIS receipt notices were nonetheless detained.

After Detention: Employer Implications

If an employee is detained at an airport, the consequences extend well beyond a missed flight. After initial processing, a detained individual may be transferred to a detention facility that is not near the airport of encounter, and in some cases not in the same state, making it difficult for family members, employers, or attorneys to locate them quickly. ICE maintains an online detainee locator that allows searches by name and country of birth, but the tool is not updated in real time, and a detained individual may not appear in the system for hours or even days after the initial encounter.

ICE may serve a detained person with a Notice to Appear (NTA), initiating formal removal proceedings, but the hearing date listed on the NTA is typically a placeholder. The immigration court may take several weeks to schedule the first hearing. During this period, the individual may request release on bond, but bond is not guaranteed and is unavailable to certain categories of detainees.

For employers, the immediate impact is the sudden, unplanned absence of an employee who may have been traveling for business with no clear timeline for resolution. Employers may find themselves unable to confirm even the basic status of a detained worker.

At-risk employees may wish to pre-sign a privacy waiver that designates a trusted contact, such as an attorney or family member, as an authorized recipient of case information. Employees should also consider sharing their immigration attorney’s contact details with a colleague or family member before any travel.

Who is Most at Risk?

Certain individuals with pending Form I-485 Adjustment of Status (AOS) applications:

Individuals with pending AOS applications who lack current valid visa status (I-94) have become a target for enforcement action.

This includes individuals who have previously held a nonimmigrant visa status, such as H-1B, L-1, TN, O-1 and similar categories, and who have received an EAD and/or Advance Parole while an AOS application is pending, but who have not maintained their underlying nonimmigrant status.

Individuals with pending submissions requesting certain immigration benefits, including Form I-129 petitions and Form I-539 applications, who experience a lapse in nonimmigrant status (expiration of I-94) as they await adjudication of these submissions by USCIS, have become a target for enforcement action.

Individuals with pending applications for asylum or other humanitarian protections.

Individuals with prior removal orders, certain criminal histories (including old or minor convictions or charges that were ultimately dropped), or prior immigration violations.

Recommended Employer Actions

Assessment

Conduct a comprehensive audit of the immigration status of all sponsored employees to identify individuals whose I-94 has expired, or will expire before an anticipated adjudication date.

Where eligible, consider upgrading pending USCIS filings to premium processing to accelerate adjudication timelines and reduce the period during which an employee's Form I-94 may be expired. Premium processing is available for certain Form I-129, Form I-539, and Form I-140 petitions. USCIS typically takes action within 15 or 45 business days, depending on the form type. Shortening the pendency window can reduce an employee's exposure to enforcement action during the gap between filing and a decision.

For employment-based applicants, evaluate whether it is possible to maintain underlying nonimmigrant status (e.g., H-1B, L-1, O-1) rather than relying solely on an EAD or advance parole while an Adjustment of Status application is pending.

Pre-Travel Measures

Advise at-risk employees to defer non-essential air travel, including both domestic and international flights.

Notify immigration counsel before any essential air travel so that a case-specific risk-assessment can be conducted in advance.

Employee Readiness

Encourage traveling employees to have a complete set of immigration documents accessible at all times, including receipt notices (Form I-797) for all pending applications, EADs, valid Advance Parole documents, a valid passport, prior visa stamps, and evidence of current employment.

Recommend that employees store copies of all immigration documents in a secure location accessible to a trusted family member or designated contact, and that they familiarize themselves with available resources on how to prepare for a potential enforcement encounter.

Employees should ensure a trusted individual is listed as an emergency contact with the employer so that HR or legal can reach them promptly in the event of detention.

Employer Preparedness for Detention

Develop an internal protocol for responding to an employee placed in detention, including a designated point of contact in HR or legal, familiarity with the ICE detainee locator, and a plan for communicating with the employee's family.

Consider implementing a policy addressing the employment status of employees who are detained, including whether to place a detained employee on a defined leave period (e.g., 30, 60, or 90 days) before making any separation decisions. A clear policy established in advance can help ensure consistent treatment, reduce legal risk, and provide detained employees a reasonable window to resolve their immigration matters.

Looking Ahead

This Legal Update reflects a rapidly evolving enforcement landscape, and guidance may change as further information becomes available. We will continue to monitor developments and provide updates.

text:
Linda Wolff said she was recording a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operation in Inwood Thursday when a masked federal agent sprayed her with a chemical irritant.

“He was walking toward me, and I was like, ‘He’s not going to mace me,’” she said.

Wolff had confronted a tow truck driver who arrived after two vehicles used by federal agents appeared to have flat tires.

Seconds later, the agent walked toward Wolff and sprayed her.

She said her sunglasses partially protected her eyes, and the adrenaline kept her recording the scene on her phone.

“It was all over my hair, my face, my lips, my clothes, my hands,” Wolff said.

By Friday, Wolff was back on so-called ICE watch, but this time in Elmhurst.

The Upper West Side resident and other volunteers track immigration enforcement reports, warn neighbors and document agents.

“We’re training them to document, document, document. Stay back and document,” Wolff said.

In Inwood, City Councilwoman Carmen De La Rosa spent the day handing residents pamphlets with information so they know their rights.

“The fear is real. We can feel it in our community as we’re a majority immigrant community,” she said.

De La Rosa said that’s why she’s taking the information directly to residents, hoping they’re prepared before ICE shows up at their door.

“I’m very cautious for myself, my family members,” Inwood resident Robert Arzola said.

“Every day, there’s a sighting of some sort. Yesterday’s escalation, I felt, was not normal,” De La Rosa said.

For Wolff, Thursday’s confrontation is now heading to court.

She said she plans to sue and says being sprayed won’t stop her from documenting future ICE operations.

“This isn’t violent. We’re not violent,” Wolff said.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security did not respond to NY1’s inquiry regarding this story.

In a separate inquiry response, the agency blamed the state’s policies limiting cooperation with federal immigration authorities.

Alexandra Lozano was based in Washington state but operated offices across the country, including in Houston's East End.

A federal lawsuit filed in Washington state by more than 100 former clients accuses her of lying on Violence Against Women Act (VAWA) petitions to stay in the country, which are meant for victims of domestic violence.

The suit claims that in one video posted to social media, Lozano said that typical family arguments could count as abuse.

"For people to be taking advantage of this is the lowest of the low," said Cesar Espinosa with advocacy group FIEL.

Espinosa says he's been in contact with former Lozano clients from Houston. He said many are now trying to obtain a U-visa designed for crime victims since they claim they were victims of Lozano's fraud.

"We've already had about five to 10 people who have been picked up by ICE because of these fraudulent claims," Espinosa said.

In a statement to ABC13's sister station KABC in Los Angeles, Lozano's attorney wrote:

"Alexandra denies the allegations that have been raised by a small number of the thousands of individuals she has represented. She will address those allegations fully in court."

According to the lawsuit, clients claim their signatures were added to documents they never signed.

The suit accuses Lozano's firm of "narrative engineering to generate ... fabricated humanitarian claims at scale."

A review by the Washington State Disciplinary Board found Lozano's signature on almost 54,000 pending immigration petitions.

"If immigration interprets it as though the client was trying to commit a fraud and not the attorney, this could lead to a deportation," Espinosa said.

The suit said Lozano was charging clients between $10,000 and $25,000.

In many cases, it said that clients would meet with salespeople instead of actual attorneys.

text:
EL PASO, Texas (Border Report) — Estrella del Paso, a full-service immigration legal aid agency serving low-income immigrants and refugees, has shut down its legal program for unaccompanied migrant children after the Trump administration declined to renew its federal contract and withheld nearly $1 million in reimbursements for legal services the nonprofit says it already completed.

“The federal government is withholding close to a million dollars in payments for legal services that we already provided to unaccompanied children,” Executive Director Melissa M. Lopez said in a statement Friday. “Without payment from the federal government, we simply can’t operate this program.”

The program officially closed Friday, July 31, leaving 13 employees without jobs and jeopardizing legal representation for hundreds of migrant children in the immigration courts in the area. Currently, Estrella El Paso represents about 243 unaccompanied migrant children in court.

Lopez added that the federal administration is “demanding confidential client information that has no right to,” and that “they will not breach their legal or ethical obligations as attorneys by disclosing confidential information.”

For nearly 20 years, Congress has funded legal representation for unaccompanied migrant children, many of whom fled violence, trafficking, or persecution. Estrella del Paso said those services are required under federal law and help children navigate the complex immigration court system.

“We have an ethical, legal and moral obligation to continue representing these children,” Lopez said. “With or without money from the federal government, we must do that.”

Estrella del Paso said the federal government currently owes the organization nearly $1 million for legal work already completed under its contract. That amount is expected to increase once the nonprofit submits invoices for services provided in July.

According to the organization, the dispute extends beyond El Paso. Estrella del Paso said the administration has withheld approximately $65 million in payments owed to a nationwide network of more than 90 nonprofit legal service providers that represent unaccompanied migrant children.

Lopez said the loss of funding threatens to dismantle decades of specialized experience serving traumatized children.

“Over the course of 20 years, this network of legal service providers has developed a unique level of expertise working with children who have experienced trauma,” she said. “We know what happens to children who go to court without an attorney. In one word, it is deportation.”

The nonprofit said children who appear in immigration court without legal representation rarely succeed in their cases. It estimates more than 20,000 unaccompanied migrant children nationwide could be affected by the funding dispute.

Despite the closure of the program, Lopez said Estrella del Paso intends to continue representing its current clients and appealed to the community for support.

“We need your help to make sure we keep our doors open and continue to see through our responsibility to these children,” she said.

Lopez added that children without a lawyer win the right to stay less than 1% of the time.

The federal government has not publicly responded to Estrella del Paso’s latest announcement.

title: United States | USCIS posts update on TPS designations for Ethiopia, South Sudan and Yemen
text:
U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services published updates on the termination of Temporary Protected Status (TPS) designations for Ethiopia and South Sudan, extending the validity dates for Employment Authorization Documents (EADs) per respective court orders. USCIS also announced that EADs with category A12 or C19 issued to TPS beneficiaries from Yemen are no longer valid, as the country’s TPS designation is terminated.

Key takeaways:

In the alert posted for Yemen, USCIS states “the Yemen TPS designation is terminated, effective July 20, 2026. Employers [completing Form I-9] must reverify TPS Yemen beneficiaries who presented these EADs and cannot continue employing a person who does not provide proof of current employment authorization.”

In the respective alerts posted for Ethiopia and South Sudan to the agency’s I-9 Central webpage, USCIS directs employers that “[w]hen completing the Expiration Date (if any) fields on Form I-9, input ‘as per court order’ in Section 1 and ‘Aug. 6, 2026’ in Section 2 along with a note in the additional information box. Employers may download the Alert and TPS [designated country] webpage and attach them to Form I-9. When completing a case in E-Verify, enter the expiration date of ‘Aug. 6, 2026’ from the Form I-9. Check USCIS websites regularly for updated information.”

Both updates state that the extensions are “limited relief until the lower courts align with the U.S. Supreme Court’s favorable decision in Mullin v. Doe, 609 U.S. (2026), issued on June 25, 2026.”

Ethiopia: According to the update, “The validity of Employment Authorization Documents (EADs) issued under the TPS designation of Ethiopia with an original expiration date of June 12, 2024, and Dec. 12, 2025, is extended per court order. African Communities Together et al. v. Noem et al., No. 26-cv-10278-BEM (D. Mass.).”

South Sudan: According to the update, “The validity of Employment Authorization Documents (EADs) issued under the TPS designation of South Sudan with an original expiration date of Nov. 3, 2023, May 3, 2025, or Nov. 3, 2025, is extended per court order. African Communities Together et al. v. Noem et al., No. 25-cv-13939-PBS (D. Mass.).”

Additional Information: The updates for Ethiopia, South Sudan and Yemen supersede the guidance issued on July 17. Individuals should continue to check the respective USCIS TPS country pages for current information.

This alert has been provided by the BAL U.S. Practice Group.

text:
A group of human rights organizations is seeking the immediate release of a breastfeeding mother with a pending asylum claim who was detained in May by immigration agents at her home in Nashville as she was putting her two young children into a car to get to a doctor's appointment.

In a complaint filed Wednesday with the Department of Homeland Security's Office of Inspector General, the organizations allege that Immigration and Customs Enforcement is violating its own policies against detaining pregnant, postpartum and nursing parents and requiring ICE to facilitate visits between children and parents.

The woman, whose name is redacted in the five-page complaint, is being held in a Louisiana facility 700 miles from Nashville and has not seen her children since her May 19 arrest, the complaint said. She has no criminal record.

The woman has had a pending asylum claim after clearing a "credible fear" interview with immigration officials after she entered the United States from Guatemala in 2022 -- the initial threshold necessary to establish an asylum case, according to the complaint filed by organizations including Amnesty International, the Kennedy Human Rights Center and the Tennessee Immigration & Refugee Rights Coalition.

At the time of her arrest, she was breastfeeding both of her daughters, a then-8-month-old infant and a 2-year-old toddler who has Down syndrome and multiple medical conditions.

"The separation of an infant from a nursing mother, and of a medically fragile toddler from her primary caregiver, causes significant and ongoing harm to all three family members," the complaint said.

"We implore DHS to act immediately," the complaint continued. "Every day of delay increases the risk of irreversible harm to (the woman) and her two U.S. citizen children."

Other organizations signing onto the complaint are Sanctuary of the South, Southern Poverty Law Center and the ACLU of Louisiana, where the woman is entering her third month of detention.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said the woman "chose to leave her two children with an adult at the home" when she was detained.

"On May 19, ICE detained a criminal illegal alien from Guatemala while serving a federal warrant at her residence in Nashville," an email from the spokesperson said. "The illegal alien, with previous charges for falsely claiming US citizenship, chose to leave her two children with an adult at the home."

The warrant was for the father of the woman's children, who was not there, according to the complaint.

The spokesperson did not respond to a request for data on the number of nursing mothers being held in immigration detention facilities but said it was not a frequent occurrence.

"Pregnant and nursing women in ICE detention are exceedingly rare. When this occurs, the women receive regular prenatal visits, mental health services, nutritional support and accommodations aligned with community standards of care." the emailed response said.

The care also includes medical, dental and mental health screenings within 12 hours of arrival at each detention facility, a full health assessment within 14 days and access to medical appointments and emergency care, the spokesperson said.

"This is the best healthcare many of these individuals have received in their entire lives," the spokesperson said.

ICE guidelines generally bar detaining nursing mothers

ICE's rules say that the agency may only detain nursing parents under narrow "exceptional circumstances" such as risks to national security or an imminent threat to others.

"Generally, ICE should not detain, arrest or take into custody for an administrative violation of the immigration laws, individuals known to be pregnant, postpartum or nursing unless release is prohibited by law or exceptional circumstances exist," the policy says.

Advocates say the agency is routinely flouting those rules, which were reinstated during the Biden administration in 2021 after the first Trump administration vacated similar rules barring the detention of pregnant, postpartum and nursing parents in 2017.

Anthony Enriquez, vice president of U.S. advocacy and litigation for the Kennedy Human Rights Center, represents two people challenging their detention under the rules for pregnant, postpartum and nursing women. The organization does not represent the mother from Nashville but joined the complaint in support.

There are likely many more pregnant, postpartum and nursing mothers being detained, but ICE is failing to follow rules that require it to keep data on the number, Enriquez said.

"How many is a question that only DHS is going to be able to answer, but I suspect it doesn't know the answer because it's not tracking that," he said. "We're just seeing flagrant violations of that directive, punishing not just the woman but the child as well'

In February, in response to a demand for data by U.S. Sen. Patty Murray, a Democrat from Washington state, ICE provided snapshot data that showed, as of Feb. 16, there were 86 pregnant women, 35 postpartum women and 15 nursing women in ICE detention.

The data includes only women in the 23 detention centers served by the ICE Health Services Corps, a medical provider that serves a fraction of ICE facilities. It does not include pregnant, postpartum and nursing detainees at more than 200 other immigration detention centers where medical care is provided by private contractors.

Enriquez said he believes there are now many more, citing litigation brought across the nation, media reports and a high volume of calls from potential clients to his organization.

He also cited a Government Accounting Office report from 2020 that tracked a steep increase in the detention of pregnant women after the first Trump administration repealed rules against it.

In 2016, before the Trump administration repealed those rules, ICE had detained 1,380 pregnant women in that year. After its repeal, it reported detaining 2,097 pregnant women in 2018.

"The reason this is important is we've seen women who have reported waiting weeks for prenatal appointments. Women have reported bleeding for days before being hospitalized or received medical follow-up up to two weeks after a miscarriage," Enriquez said.

"We've heard reports of women being shackled at their ankles, wrists and waists during medical exams," he continued. "There are reports of women not receiving adequate prenatal nutrition. And we've seen nursing mothers taken from their breastfeeding infants. Lactation is, by definition, the infant's food source, so it's punishing not just the woman but the child as well."

The advocacy organizations' complaint demands that ICE confirm in writing whether the Nashville mother meets any of the criteria of the "exceptional circumstances" required for her continued detention. It also demands her immediate release to resume nursing her children.

They have not been able to see their mother since her detention, they noted. A neighbor is caring for them both.

After more than two months in detention, the woman is "experiencing the physical effects of the abrupt cessation of breastfeeding," compounded by diabetes, the complaint said. Her oldest daughter with Down syndrome has a history of medical complications and has missed ongoing weekly therapies since her mother's detention, it said.

text:
Immigration authorities detained a 59-year-old Sunnyvale resident earlier this month and shuttled her through multiple detention centers in the days that followed, often under severe physical conditions, according to her family.

Alevtina Soboleva was at the airport in Buffalo, New York, on July 20 to board a flight back to the Bay Area after a vacation at Niagara Falls when plainclothes officers approached her for a "documents check," said Soboleva's 30-year-old daughter Daria, who was with her at the time.

At the time, the officers did not identify themselves as belonging to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement or any other immigration agency, Daria Soboleva said.

Her mother was then transported from one detention facility to another, Daria Soboleva said.

"There is no control in this situation with what's happening," she said in an interview on Thursday. "She is just moved, and I cannot find her, I cannot speak to her."

ICE records show that, as of Thursday afternoon, Alevtina is currently in custody at the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center in Basile, Louisiana. She has been in detention for 10 days.

ICE did not immediately respond to a request for comment Thursday evening on Alevtina Soboleva's case.

Daria Soboleva, a research scientist at Sunnyvale-based firm Cerebras Systems, said that her mother moved to the United States from Russia in October 2021 to help her settle into her new job.

In 2022, when war broke out between Russia and Ukraine, they decided that it was unsafe to return to Russia. In April 2022, Alevtina Soboleva filed for her asylum application, which is still pending.

"She does not have any criminal record," Daria Soboleva said Thursday. "She did everything right, and I don't understand what has happened."

After officers took custody of Alevtina Soboleva at the Buffalo airport, her daughter could not contact her for four days.

When the two finally spoke, Alevtina Soboleva had been moved to the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center.

"When she was able to speak to me for the first time, she was just crying nonstop," Daria Soboleva said. "She was so humiliated, she could never imagine being treated like this."

According to their phone conversation, Alevtina was shackled with handcuffs and chains and placed inside a cage as she was transported from one detention center to another.

The cage, Alevtina recounted to Daria, had very poor air circulation, and when she asked to be let out to breathe fresh air, she was not permitted to do so.

She was refused the use of a bathroom and had to urinate on herself. She also suffered panic attacks and was refused water when she asked for it.

"She was begging them just to wet her lips a little because she had been there for hours," said Daria. "That wasn't allowed, too."

After arriving at the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center, she complained of chills and asked for warm clothing, but was not provided any. When a fellow detainee gave her fever medication and a warm hat, authorities at the detention center took them away from her.

Now, Daria can speak with her mother but is worried about her health, given that she already suffers from vertigo.

The family has engaged their attorney as well as the office of Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Santa Clara, to expedite the proceedings and bring Alevtina back home.

"My mom is going through this, but I cannot imagine anyone's mom going through this," said Daria. "To me, it just sounds like a very, very bad nightmare."

text:
A Johns Hopkins University researcher, originally from Cameroon, was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers at Baltimore Washington International Airport earlier this week, according to the university, which said it is "deeply concerned" about the matter.

According to a DHS spokesperson, ICE agents arrested Fatima Ameaka, a Cameroonian national at the airport on Tuesday. The spokesperson said Ameaka overstayed a visa that expired June 13, 2024.

"In violation of our nation's laws, she overstayed her visa. She will remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings," the DHS spokesperson said.

According to documents obtained by ABC News, Ameaka had a work authorization permit until 2029 and a pending asylum case.

Johns Hopkins said Ameaka, who has a doctoral degree in pharmacy, is an employee at the Bloomberg School of Public Health and is "a respected member of our community."

"The university understands the fear and concern this instills in members of our community. Dr. Ameaka was traveling in a personal capacity, and though we cannot comment on the specifics of her situation, we want to assure our community that the university is actively working to provide support for Dr. Ameaka, including ensuring she has access to legal representation," a Johns Hopkins spokesperson said.

Ameaka's arrest comes days after ABC News obtained a memo detailing federal immigration authorities' new efforts to ramp up arrests at airports of people who have allegedly overstayed their visas.

Dr. Tom Inglesby, the director of the Center for Health Security at Johns Hopkins School of Public Health, where Ameaka works, said she attended the university as a Fulbright Scholar and began working with the center two years ago, focusing on researching how to improve responses to infections disease outbreaks such as measles.

"She is an amazing person, she is really smart. She's committed and she is funny," Dr. Inglesby said in an interview.

"She's a beloved colleague at our center," he said.

Inglesby said her family and lawyers have been unable to reach her.

Ameaka is currently being held at the Alexandria Staging Facility in Louisiana, according to her attorney.

A GoFundMe page has been set up to help with her legal defense.

text:
FRESNO, Calif. (KFSN) -- A group of former clients has filed a lawsuit accusing immigration attorney Alexandra Lozano, who marketed herself as the "Miracle Lawyer," of defrauding thousands of her vulnerable immigrant clients.

According to the complaint, Lozano used religious imagery, including La Virgen de Guadalupe, in her marketing while allegedly charging clients thousands of dollars for immigration services. The lawsuit was filed by dozens of former clients represented by attorney Vicente Omar Barraza.

"She found this market, a vulnerable market, a fearful market, a desperate market, and created a system that reported with religious imagery to produce miracles, and now their miracles are turning into nightmares," Barraza said.

The complaint alleges Lozano filed fraudulent immigration documents and used unauthorized electronic signatures. Barraza said the firm concentrated on specific immigration cases because they generated higher fees.

"She focused on VAWA and T Visa cases because she could charge more and then most of the work appears to have been done in Columbia in Mexico," Barraza said.

The allegations come as Action News has learned Lozano maintained a multimillion-dollar real estate portfolio and traveled in a pink private jet valued at about $25 million.

Barraza said the alleged practices have had serious consequences for clients seeking legal status in the United States.

"All they really want to do is the right thing," Barraza said. "People not only have invested sometimes their life savings in finding a path towards legalization, but now their situation may be worse off."

Lozano's law firm is based in Seattle. Action News visited her Fresno office, where no one answered the door. Large "for lease" signs were displayed in the windows, though her name and logo remained visible inside.

"I'm certain there's probably thousands of victims in California and maybe a couple hundred if not more in the Fresno area," Barraza said.

Fresno immigration attorney Gregory Olson said several of Lozano's former clients have sought assistance from his office.

"They've all been trusting this attorney to take care of them and now they're finding out this attorney was lying or creating lies with their name signed at the bottom," Olson said.

Amid a pending investigation, Lozano has voluntarily surrendered her law license.

In a statement to Action News, her attorney said: "Alexandra denies the allegations that have been raised by a small number of the thousands of individuals she has represented. She will address those allegations fully in court."

Legal experts say the case could have far-reaching consequences given the size of Lozano's client base.

"I'm not sure that the market of immigration attorneys can absorb 35,000 cases filed by this firm. I think a lot of people are going to find themselves without representation and facing deportation," Barraza said.

You can still submit interest to join this lawsuit if you believe you or someone you know is a victim.

text:
The various sides involved in a stalemate over a case of tuberculosis in the immigrant detention facility, the GEO Aurora ICE Processing Center, faced off in federal court Friday.

GEO Group, which runs the facility and others around the country, filed a lawsuit last month against the state to stop enforcement of a new law which requires regular health and safety inspections of immigrant detention facilities.

GEO's attorney, Fred Yarger, of Denver firm Wheeler Trigg O’Donnell, argued the law unfairly singles out GEO and federal law reigns supreme. So the state doesn't have the authority to conduct the enhanced oversight, he said, including stepped up inspections and fines, spelled out in the new law.

“They know they can’t sue ICE (U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement), so they’re suing us instead,” Yarger told U.S. District Court Judge Daniel D. Domenico.

Attorneys for Colorado, from the Attorney General’s office, as well as Adams County, argued health departments for both do have clear authority to oversee public health.

The case comes amidst growing scrutiny nationally over conditions for detainees in federal immigration detention facilities and public health’s role in protecting detainees, detention center employees and the broader community from communicable diseases.

ICE did not have an attorney present at the hearing.

Domenico, a Trump appointee who has been nominated to Denver’s federal appeals court, didn’t issue a ruling, and gave no indication when he would.

CPR requested comment from both GEO and ICE about the hearing. Neither have yet responded.

ICE has provided the bare minimum of information about the TB case, saying the Aurora facility currently doesn’t have “any confirmed active tuberculosis (TB) cases.” A spokesman said it did have one case June 25, and the person was “treated, cleared and removed.”

Neither GEO nor ICE have provided a paper trail or documentation about what’s been done to respond and who was exposed, something Gov. Jared Polis, a Democrat, urged earlier this week.

What’s happening inside?

The human impact of conditions inside the GEO facility in Aurora,came into clear view outside the courtroom.

After the hearing, Jeanette Vizguerra, a high profile immigrants rights advocate and former detainee, confronted GEO's attorney in the hall.

"Do you have any idea of what's happening inside? I have idea. You no have idea," said Vizguerra, who was released just before Christmas last year, as a pair of other advocates recorded video of the encounter over cellphones and also asked pointed questions.

Yarger, and a pair of other GEO lawyers, didn't respond and retreated from an elevator back down the hall toward the courtroom. CPR reached out to Yarger. He declined comment and forwarded the request to GEO, which hasn’t yet responded.

Later, in the courtyard in front of the courthouse, Vizguerra decried conditions inside the facility and said she's heard from detainees about many more TB cases.

“Really I'm very angry,” Vizguerra said, noting the corporation operates for-profit private prisons for the government and wants immunity from responsibility for what happens to people inside. Vizguerra came to Colorado from Mexico in 1997.

“They not pay penalties. They not have regulation. They not have inspections,” Vizguerra said. “The construction (industry) have regulations. Hotels have regulation. Restaurants have regulation. For what, GEO detention centers not have regulation?”

Earlier this year the U.S. recently recorded the deadliest year for people in immigration detention in more than 20 years, with 23 deaths. Vizguerra said she’s worried the TB situation in the Aurora facility could cause more.

“How many more people need (to) die for somebody (to) take responsibility? Please, I need (people to) listen. The community need (to) listen,” she said, with tears welling up at one point. “This is human persons. This is not business. Please, somebody need to stop everything.”

Vizguerra said she’s been communicating with detainees inside, and some who have been released who describe horrid conditions and a dozen more cases. The Guardian reported earlier this month that a TB outbreak in the Aurora immigration facility has sickened at least a dozen detainees.

“But more people have very much cough,” she said. “It's coming (up) blood. Some people have very bad infection in your feet.”

Also, Vizguerra said detainees face intense heat, as summer temperatures have hit intense highs, with many days in the 90s and approaching triple digits.

“The people sometimes not have AC right now. The temperatures is 100 degrees. It's not possible to repair the AC,” she said.

Neither GEO nor ICE have responded to questions from CPR about more cases being identified inside the facility.

Adams County provides new details

For the first time since the standoff began, the leader of Adams County Health Department provided her perspective.

Kelly Weidenbach, executive director, said after a lab test confirmed a case of TB inside the facility, Adams County public health investigators started a routine effort to track the cases and see if other people had been exposed. But GEO stopped communicating. At all, she said, speaking outside the Alfred A. Arraj Courthouse in downtown Denver.

“What makes this case different from previous communicable disease investigations is just the fact that the facility has gone completely quiet and is not communicating whatsoever,” she said, “which is different than previous situations that we've been in.”

Without that, it’s virtually impossible to know what’s happening inside the facility, which has capacity for more than a thousand detainees.

“We don't know what's going on in the facility without that communication and cooperation,” Weidenbach said.

She declined to comment about the legal fight over the new state law.

“We believe we have the legal right to investigate and we believe our residents support this kind of comprehensive disease control, irrespective of the setting in which it is occurring,” she said.

Weidenbach gave details of the weeks-long TB saga. She said June 11, her agency was notified of a case of suspected TB. She said Denver Health’s Tuberculosis Program provided clinical advice and medical recommendations to GEO. A lab confirmed the case June 22. She later noted that the agency believes the person was infected with TB before entering the detention center.

“Our teams moved very quickly,” she said.

As part of its investigation, the health department followed routine protocols, requested medical records and an interview with the TB patient, access to parts of the facility where the person was housed, and complete information about people who may have been exposed, including detainees, staff and visitors.

“Those requests are routine and necessary components of any thorough tuberculosis contact investigation,” she said, noting their motivations were simple. “Allow us access to records, not to assign blame, but to verify that the threat is no longer active and proper protocols were followed,” she said.

When GEO didn’t provide information needed to complete the investigation, Adams County issued a public health order June 25th to require compliance. The Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment followed with its own written request for the same records, contact tracing information and access to the facility Adams County requested on July 14.

She said the nature of the disease makes it an important one to track and prevent.

“Tuberculosis is a very serious respiratory infection and very severe cases can lead to death. It's an infection that has a high fatality rate if left untreated,” she said, noting it may take months to years for someone who has been exposed to develop active symptoms and disease.

Weidenbach said protecting the health of the public, including stopping the spread of disease, is the agency’s mission.

“It's a large facility and we have employees, we have visitors, legal counsel for detainees and many other different people, contractors, delivery people, all sorts of people coming in and out of the facility,” she said.

text:
(NewsNation) — The Trump administration’s crackdown on illegal immigration is again focusing on the nation’s interior, surging more federal officers and agents across the United States, including to America’s airports.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers have been deployed to at least 15 airports after entering an agreement with the Transportation Security Administration that allows the two federal agencies to share data, according to multiple media reports. ABC News reported that the tactic has led to at least 27 arrests since the operation began.

The pact is making it easier for ICE to identify immigrants who are in the United States illegally, including those who overstayed visas that previously gave them a legal pathway to remain in the country.

However, the Department of Homeland Security is now ramping up efforts to detain those individuals, including at airports. DHS officials said this week they have ended policies introduced under the Biden administration that allowed immigrants in the country illegally to travel around the country.

In a statement, DHS says the only flights those immigrants are now welcome on are those bound for those leaving the United States.

Under federal immigration laws, those who overstay their visas are considered immediately deportable, which makes them a target of an administration that has vowed the largest mass domestic deportation mission in modern history.

“Temporary means temporary, and these visa applicants told the federal government when applying for the visa that they would return home when the visa expired,” said Lora Ries, the director of a border security and immigration center at the Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank. “And if they didn’t do that, they lied to the government, and they are now deportable.”

The airport enforcement effort included the arrest of a Johns Hopkins University researcher this week after she was detained in Baltimore for allegedly overstaying her visa.

In addition to sending ICE into airports, where they previously were sent to assist TSA agents during the government shutdown, the Trump administration is also changing how it is handling some cases of migrants seeking asylum.

Under a new U.S, Citizenship and Immigration Services rule, asylum officers can now refer certain affirmative asylum cases directly to immigration judges without first conducting an interview — a move the administration says will help reduce the backlog. Critics argue it removes an important step in the process and raises due process concerns.

Migrants, however, awaiting asylum hearings and other immigration-related matters that require them to appear in court have faced long delays that can often go on for years. But as the administration pushes to deport more immigrants who are either convicted criminals, face pending charges, or have overstayed previous orders for removal, the administration is seeking to quickly remove those immigrants rather than allowing them to stay in the U.S. as they wait out the process.

Yet, Julia Gelatt, the associate director of the Migration Policy Institute’s U.S. Program, told NewsNation this week that shortening wait times for immigrants seeking a legal pathway to remain in the United States is part of the reason for much-needed reform to U.S. immigration legislation.

Gelatt was part of an MPI study this week showing that the population of unauthorized immigrants living in the United States reached a new peak of 15.8 million in 2024, after remaining around 11 million for years. The study found that about 5 million unauthorized immigrants remained in the United States between 2019 and 2024.

“Many people are trying to follow the rules of our immigration system as they understand them, but are caught somewhere in the process and haven’t yet gotten either an answer that tells them to go home or (about) some kind of permanent protection in the U.S.,” Gelatt told NewsNation Thursday.

“We really need to give people faster answers. People shouldn’t need to wait four years to see if they get asylum. If we can get timely and fair answers to people, I think that would send a message back to the sending country … of who can and can’t come to the United States.”

DHS officials insist that they are not speeding up removals, but they are also not rushing to build new detention centers. Instead, they’re expanding the use of existing state and county facilities to quickly detain and remove people already in the system

At the same time, Trump administration officials are also doubling down on pushing immigrants who may be facing removal to self-deport. After a Supreme Court ruling this week allowed the administration to move forward with ending Temporary Protective Status for immigrants from Haiti and Syria, DHS encouraged those individuals to return home on their own, promising a free plane ticket and a $2,600 check.

DHS says that during President Donald Trump’s first year back in office, more than three million migrants have left the United States, including an estimated 2.2 million who self-deported.

Still, those numbers haven’t kept White House border czar Tom Homan and senior adviser Stephen Miller from pushing for ICE to make more arrests. NewsNation reported earlier this week that ICE began an enforcement operation in New York City, which Homan said could spread to other cities as the crackdown continues.

text:
José Gregorio González is inside an immigration detention center almost a year after he donated his kidney to save the life of his brother, who has end-stage renal disease.

The Venezuelan man was taken into ICE custody July 21 during a routine check-in appointment with immigration authorities in Chicago.

González had been reporting to Immigration and Customs Enforcement since April on a weekly basis, sometimes more than once. The agency had placed him in an intensive supervision program to monitor his whereabouts after his yearlong humanitarian parole expired, according to his lawyer and brother.

“I don’t really see a need to necessarily detain him,” said Peter Meinecke, an attorney handling his immigration case and the managing attorney at Resurrection Project, a nonprofit group in Chicago.

“He has no criminal record and has been dutifully complying with supervision,” Meinecke told NBC News.

José Alfredo Pacheco, González’s younger brother and the recipient of his kidney, had just finished a follow-up medical appointment to monitor his recovery from the transplant he received last August. He texted González to let him know he was on his way to pick him up from his ICE check-in.

“Three minutes later, he replied, ‘Brother, I love you. They’re about to deport me.’ That was the only thing he wrote to me,” Pacheco told Noticias Telemundo in Spanish on Wednesday.

“My world came crashing down,” he said, noting that González is his sole caregiver. “My biggest fear is being left alone here.”

González’s story first made headlines in March 2025, when ICE detained him before he could donate his kidney to Pacheco. Community members in the Chicago area rallied in support of the brothers and advocated for González’s release under humanitarian parole. The brothers share the same mother.

González was temporarily released from ICE detention that April, and the brothers successfully underwent a lifesaving kidney transplant surgery in August.

“Someone who’s committed a very selfless act, like donating a kidney, is still being treated like they’re a threat to this country,” Meinecke said. “It’s an alarming precedent to be setting in terms of how we’re treating immigrants in this country.”

According to the Department of Homeland Security, González first attempted to enter the U.S. in June 2023, but Border Patrol arrested him and removed him from the country.

In December 2023, Pacheco was diagnosed with end-stage renal disease. González returned to the U.S. a month later, in January 2024, to care for his brother, who at the time needed four-hour dialysis sessions three times a week.

“In violation of our nation’s laws, he illegally re-entered the country,” a DHS spokesperson said about González’s January 2024 entry into the U.S.

González sought asylum but did not pass an initial credible fear interview, so immigration authorities placed a deportation order on him. Still, he was allowed to remain in the country under ICE supervision and with an ankle monitor to track him, which is not uncommon.

Before González’s humanitarian parole was set to expire in April, Meinecke said he filed a request to temporarily stop the government from enforcing the deportation order against his client.

That application was still pending when ICE detained González last week, Meinecke said.

According to the DHS spokesperson, González overstayed his parole in “violation of our nation’s laws.”

Meinecke said they intend to try to request another humanitarian parole for release from detention.

“While his health has more or less progressed the way you would hope following a surgery,” the attorney said about González, “his brother’s hasn’t been as straightforward.”

Pacheco said he has had two setbacks on the delicate journey to recovery from his kidney transplant. The worse one, a severe blood infection, landed him in the hospital in January. When he felt like he almost didn’t make it, Pacheco said his brother “was the only one who was with me.”

As a living organ donor, González is also under structured medical supervision to ensure his remaining kidney adapts well, Pacheco said. “He still has to attend his medical appointments, and there is no health care in Venezuela,” he said.

Venezuela’s fragile health care system had been deteriorating for years before two powerful earthquakes rattled the South American nation last month, killing more than 5,000 people and further exacerbating its ongoing health crisis.

The DHS spokesperson said González will “remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings” to Venezuela.

On Sunday, Pacheco spoke to González, who called him from an immigration detention center in Missouri, where he is being held. Pacheco said his older brother never complained about the situation and instead insisted he not worry about him.

“It’s very hard when we siblings are so close,” Pacheco said with emotion. “We would give our lives for one another. … He is the best of us all.”
